item.title: At today's Triple-i Showcase, Dave the Diver studio Mintrocket announced a surprisingly obvious, and perfectly fitting, collaboration. The game's final DLC, set for release in early 2027, brings the worlds of Subnautica 2 and Dave the Diver together. Read more
item.description:
At today's Triple-i Showcase, Dave the Diver studio Mintrocket announced a surprisingly obvious, and perfectly fitting, collaboration. The game's final DLC, set for release in early 2027, brings the worlds of Subnautica 2 and Dave the Diver together.
Although the two games share deep-sea exploration as a mechanic, they're at opposite ends of the spectrum tonally - though they're still a better fit than many of the other brands Dave the Diver has crossed over with. These have included Balatro, Yakuza, Godzilla, and Guilty Gear to name a few.
The upcoming Subnautica 2 DLC is free and was developed in collaboration with Subnautica 2 team Unknown Worlds. It brings Subnautica 2's ocean moon of Proteus to Dave the Diver, and sees Dave and Bancho - having discovered all species of sea creatures and associated sushi recipes in this dimension - travel to a new dimension to uncover more.
While there, yes, they're going to run into Subnautica 2's iconic Leviathan, but also make new friends and hopefully return home having made a lot of new discoveries. Jaeho Hwang, Mintrocket studio director said: "Both games are set underwater, but Subnautica has such a distinct approach to underwater exploration, so working with the Subnautica 2 team gave us a chance to bring a new wave to Dave the Diver experience."
Subnautica 2 creative director Anthony Gallegos added: "It’s clear that we both adore one another’s games a lot, and the expansion is a love letter to both Dave the Diver and the Subnautica universe. People are in for a treat."
The Subnautica 2 x Dave the Diver crossover DLC is available to wishlist on Steam now. Subnautica 2, which launched in early access this year, has been incredibly successful. It sold more than 5 million copies in under a month, convincing publisher Krafton - which was embroiled in a legal battle with studio founders before launch - to turn it into a "franchise IP".

item.title: Former Activision boss Bobby Kotick has returned to a position of high influence as a board member of Skydance, the new entertainment juggernaut formed by the merging of Warner Bros. into Paramount. Read more
item.description:
Former Activision boss Bobby Kotick has returned to a position of high influence as a board member of Skydance, the new entertainment juggernaut formed by the merging of Warner Bros. into Paramount.
Kotick, who stepped down as Activision CEO following Xbox's $68.7bn acquisition of the company back in 2023, is joining the 13-person board alongside a selection of other newcomers. These include former UK prime minister Tony Blair, who is joining in an advisor role, and philanthropist Laurene Powell.
David Ellison, architect of the Warner Bros / Paramount merger, and Skydance's newly crowned CEO, issued the following statement: "I am delighted to welcome Laurene and Bobby to our Board and honored to have Tony join us as an Advisor. Bobby led a global entertainment company through three decades of sustained growth, and he brings real perspective on building enduring franchises and connecting with fans.
"His record of pairing bold strategic moves with disciplined capital allocation is exactly the experience we need as we bring our businesses together. Tony has led at the highest levels of government, respected for his intellect, strategic vision and ability to bring people together around bold, forward-looking ideas. His global perspective and insight will be invaluable as we turn ambition into results."
This merger has also resulted in the video game arms of both Warner Bros and Paramount being combined. Per Variety, the Skydance gaming division is now led by Tony Driscoll, who previously launched Fortnite's creator economy and ecosystem initiative between 2021 and 2024. That conjoined games divisions will have a variety of franchises at its fingertips, including Mortal Kombat, Mission Impossible, Avatar: The Last Airbender, and Harry Potter through Hogwarts Legacy 2.
In an email sent to staff and seen by Variety, Skydance president Andy Gordon wrote: "We're investing in our future growth engines alongside our core ambitions in TV, Film and direct-to-consumer: Games, Experiences, Consumer Products, and Publishing. These are core pillars of our strategy to build engagement and fandom in both the physical and digital worlds. We want to meet consumers where they watch, play, and engage. At the same time, we see opportunities to build on DC Comics' storytelling and expand our e-commerce offerings to connect fans with the brands they love."
Warner Bros has a lengthy, albeit rocky, history with video game development. While it has overseen some popular releases including Hogwarts Legacy and numerous Mortal Kombat games, recent years have not been as fruitful. Warner Bros Montreal suffered layoffs earlier this year, and Suicide Squad: Kill the Justice League developer Rocksteady was ravaged by staffing cuts in recent years.
Paramount, on the other hand, has a much more fledgling video games division. Its latest game, Avatar Legends: The Fighting game, has proven a niche yet adored release to genre diehards. Aside from that, it is also working with Platinum Games on TMNT: The Last Ronin, though a release date has yet to be announced.
Bobby Kotick led Activision during a period when the state of California sued the company for what it alleged was a "frat boy" company culture which created a "breeding ground for harassment and discrimination against women". Later, a Wall Street Journal report alleged that "Kotick knew for years about sexual-misconduct allegations". Bobby Kotick continues to deny the claims made in this Wall Street Journal report.
The report itself claims Kotick "received a troubling email in July 2018", and that "A lawyer for a former employee at Sledgehammer Games, an Activision-owned studio, alleged in the email that her client had been raped in 2016 and 2017 by her male supervisor after she had been pressured to consume too much alcohol in the office and at work events."
The Wall Street Journal claims this employee "reported the incidents to Sledgehammer's human-resources department and other supervisors, but nothing happened, according to the email, which threatened a lawsuit against the company."
It also reports that within months of receiving this email "Activision reached an out-of-court settlement with the woman, who also had reported one of the incidents to the police," and that "Kotick didn't inform the company’s board of directors about the alleged rapes or the settlement," according to people with knowledge of the board.
Last month, People Make Games released its own report focusing on Kotick's legal team's response to this report in the years since it was published. The PMG report, authored by journalist Mikhail Klimentov, cites a source who told Klimentov they had "received a letter from a defamation firm representing Bobby Kotick." This source, themself a journalist, had previously covered the Wall Street Journal's investigation into Kotick. Kliemtov said "this defamation firm was demanding that my source change their story", and that the firm representing Kotick had claimed the Wall Street Journal investigation "had been 'disproven'."
Klimentov also reported this legal letter "referenced a handful of other websites and publications that had seemingly given into this defamation firm's demands: Striking language the firm didn't like, adding editor's notes that referred to the Journal's investigation as 'debunked', and in at least one case deleting an article entirely."
Despite these claims, however, the original Wall Street Journal report remains live and unchanged.

item.title: Riot Games has released a final gameplay trailer for 2XKO, its short-lived fighting game set to be sunsetted later this year. The game is going out with a bang, with a shock reveal of a secret character coming alongside the games last major update. Read more
item.description:
Riot Games has released a final gameplay trailer for 2XKO, its short-lived fighting game set to be sunsetted later this year. The game is going out with a bang, with a shock reveal of a secret character coming alongside the games last major update.
This final major update, set to go live on the 27th October, was previously confirmed to feature Samira as the game's 16th character. This trailer features a showcase of her move set in action, however she shares the spotlight with Sett, a character who had been long requested from fans.
Sett, a bulky brawler, is seen to possess a combination of shattering blows and powerful grabs in this trailer. A significant difference between his 2XKO abilities and the kit available to him in League of Legends is a powered-up state which appears to intensify many of his special moves, granting them new and dangerous properties. One of his supers also appears to show him grabbing both characters on the enemy team at once, slamming them together in a homage to his MOBA manifestation.
2XKO was in development at Riot Games for a long time, and released earlier this year to much fanfare from fighting game fans. Unfortunately, the development team responsible for it almost immediately suffered layoffs, and later the 2XKO's end of service was announced as player retention was not strong enough to justify the cost of support of additional work on the game beyond its first season of character releases.
Nonetheless, it is a game with a lot of merit. It's also not vanishing forever unlike other live service games who have followed a similar path. The game will remain playable for the foreseeable future, and the microtransaction store has been taken out and replaced with an optional one-time purchase that unlocks the full suite of in-game cosmetics, save perhaps for a Chipotle promotional avatar outfit. As such, those excited by Sett's reveal can enjoy messing around with him later this month.

item.title: GTA 6 will let you listen to radio stations while not in a car, by wearing headphones and earbuds connected to smartphones. GTA 6 also introduces on-demand podcasts, so you can binge true crime while also doing true crime - something like that. Read more
item.description:
GTA 6 will let you listen to radio stations while not in a car, by wearing headphones and earbuds connected to smartphones. GTA 6 also introduces on-demand podcasts, so you can binge true crime while also doing true crime - something like that.
"For the first time ever, Grand Theft Auto 6 introduces a series of on-demand podcasts for Jason and Lucia to experience beyond Leonida's terrestrial radio," Rockstar wrote on its website, "with both radio and podcasts available to listen to in vehicles and on foot through newly introduced headphones and earbuds connected to their smartphones."
Rockstar announced these additions while detailing six of radio stations coming to GTA 6, which appear to be hosted by incredibly famous real-world singers (according to Rolling Stone), while offering musical previews of what we'll hear there.
It's an incredibly expensive line-up for a game that has been made with no expense spared. As Christian Donlan noted after watching Netflix's extended GTA 6 reveal: this is what a billion dollars gets you.
The timing of this GTA 6 announcement coincides with another huge GTA 6 gameplay footage leak by CyberLeek, which shows nudity, dirt-biking and a developer menu. CyberLeek activity had seemed to have stopped following Rockstar parent company Take-Two taking legal action to track them down and find them, but this latest development suggests they're still at large.
Meanwhile, GTA 6 edges ever closer to its 19th November release, while Rockstar Games also fights an employment tribunal case in Scotland linked to alleged union busting.

item.title: CD Projekt Red has rolled out a substantial patch for the new Witcher 3 Remastered edition of the game, notably adding more lighting-related options to the console versions of the game, such as Bloom, enabling you to turn them off, should you wish. Read more
item.description:
CD Projekt Red has rolled out a substantial patch for the new Witcher 3 Remastered edition of the game, notably adding more lighting-related options to the console versions of the game, such as Bloom, enabling you to turn them off, should you wish.
CD Projekt Red also noted it was working on an update for the Switch 2 version of The Witcher 3 Remastered to get "closer parity between all versions of the game", and to improve image "clarity and sharpness". More information on the Switch 2 patch is coming in the "following days".
Notable fixes in Witcher 3 patch 5.01 - out now on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series S/X - include fixes to dodging and odd bugs such as those where Geralt's stamina would suddenly deplete when sprinting and dodging at the same time. Player-controlled boats shouldn't "start moving uncontrollably" any more, which is a relief, ladder "interactions" have been improved, and witcher mentor Vesemir won't keep repeating himself when you cast the Quen Sign.
PC fixes address faults like incorrect graphics settings being applied - and in some circumstances the wrong GPU being selected for use, bizarrely - whereas console changes introduce promised performance improvements as well as voiceover volume improvements, and fixes for incorrect frame-rate limits being applied.

item.description:
We're big fans of Star Wars: Galactic Racer, having given the fast and punishing racing game five stars in our review. We also spoke to developer Fuse Games to better understand how it recaptured the Burnout spirit so well in the game. And it was then we heard about Fuse's unique approach to prototyping Galactic Racer.
"What's the fastest way we can get ideas down and then talk about them?" Fuse Games CEO Matt Webster told Eurogamer. "Modern engines are so capable that you can do a lot of it in-software, but there's still something [about that which is] not as fast as getting a written idea down."
Creative director Kieran Crimmin added: "There's a prototyping tool for every kind of system that you want to prototype, and the one that you pick should be the one that gets you there the quickest, and gets you to validate the emotion the quickest."
In Galactic Racers' case, the tool was a board game, which had Post-It notes stuck to it that the team used to map out the game's upgrades and meta progression systems. "I mean, I say 'board game': a lot of it is Post-Its and a scribble and some dice," Crimmins said. "But we're trying to validate those feelings as quickly as possible, o you just pick the best tool for the moment."
Elsewhere in the interview, Crimmins explained the importance of distilling game-feel in playable game prototypes and testing them quickly to see if players shared the same feelings about them.
"We like many things," Crimmins said. "We have loads of ideas, and we have references and emotions that we're trying to get to. But you can't know if you've got game-feel. You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system. So we just try and get into [the] prototype [stage], get it into our players' hands. See if they're feeling those emotions.
"Rather than worry about whether it's the right set of things," Crimmins added, "we worry about getting it as a play experience as quickly as possible and seeing if it feels right."
In the Star Wars: Galactic Racer Eurogamer review, Christian Donlan was enamoured with the game's ability to merge modern games' unlockables and Roguelite traits with the tight course design of classic games. "Galactic Racer never forgets that between the loot and the loadout and the story choices this is still a racing game. The game has that ceaseless full-ahead pelt that Burnout offers and each corner is a set-piece, even before you tip your Skim Speeder onto one edge," Donlan wrote.

item.title: The week of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ reveals continues, and the latest highlighted a questionable addition that seems to offer an unfair advantage in an extraction shooter. Read more
item.description:
The week of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ reveals continues, and the latest highlighted a questionable addition that seems to offer an unfair advantage in an extraction shooter.
The DMZ progression trailer, which went live overnight, is mainly centered around the out-of-match metagame. Between rounds, players can spend time at the Forward Operating Base (FOB) to upgrade and customise weapons, unlock new skills for their operators, create useful items using the 3D printer, and prepare for their next deployment. Much of this was revealed earlier in the week.
But one new thing that stood out was how players will load into the match - and what they can load in with. As seen in the video, there are five ways for players to 'infil' into a match, varied by cost. These range from being free to costing a whopping $100,000 in DMZ Cash per deployment.
The free option spawns your character on foot at a random point, which has long been the default option in all other extraction shooters, as it ensures players start each match equally. But Modern Warfare 4 DMZ takes that several steps further.
The next infil option costs $5,000 and spawns the squad in a Polaris Dagor A1, a tactical off-road vehicle, offering a significant speed advantage. If you're willing to spend $25,000 to deploy, meanwhile, you'll do so in a Light Tactical Vehicle (LTV), which has considerably more armour. The Call of Duty Blog says the version found across DMZ's map has an optional .50 Cal turret, but it's not clear whether the LTV you can spawn in has one.
Then there's the $50,000 option, which spawns the squad in a helicopter, which represents an enormous advantage over people spawning on foot. But by far the most ludicrous option is the $100,000 tier, an air vehicle, which looks like the cargo plane you jump out of at the start of battle royale matches in games like Warzone. This, presumably, allows the squad to pick the specific point on the map they want to start at - a luxury other players won't have as spawn points in DMZ are randomised.
Now, it's worth pointing out that unlocking the ability to spawn in the LTV and helicopter is locked behind completing a separate story mission for each option, meaning they won't immediately be available to players even if they can afford it.
That said, all of the non on-foot options offer clear advantages. A player in a buggy can zoom around the map quickly, clearing objectives one after another. A squad in a helicopter can do that even faster, potentially flying directly to a boss' spawn location to kill it and extract early. And as those vehicles persist throughout the match, it's possible - assuming they're not destroyed or abandoned - for a squad to efficiently jump between points of interest before heading to the extraction point, making for a far less risky deployment.
Incidentally, Reality, one of Call of Duty's longtime leakers, revealed these options last year, alongside DMZ's different weather conditions. In their post on X, they said the last paid spawn option - the aircraft - is an AC-130 gunship, the devastating multiplayer Killstreak with multiple heavy guns mounted on it. The AC-130 is often confused with its cargo and transport sibling the C-130, which is probably what's happened here, because starting the match with such a high-power attack vehicle would ruin the experience for all other players.
I can imagine weeks or months into DMZ's life, as players' cash reserves grow and they become more familiar with the map and where everything is, free spawns will turn into the poor, new player option, inevitably putting them at an immediate disadvantage.
How Infinity Ward balances all that remains to be seen, but seeing the confusion about the existence of a PvE-only mode within DMZ doesn't fill me with a lot of hope. DMZ launches with Modern Warfare 4 on 23rd October for PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2.

item.description:
Today, Microsoft announced it is setting up a new branch of the Xbox business named XP. In a blog over at the Xbox Wire, Microsoft details what this new area of the business looks like - it consists of four branches: Xbox Places, Xbox Pictures, Xbox Partnerships, Xbox Products.
"[XP] brings together capabilities that have existed across various teams at Xbox for years and aligns them behind a shared mission: helping our franchises reach more people, create deeper connections with players and new fans, and unlock new opportunities for these fandoms to grow around the world," says a press release from Matthew Ball, chief strategy officer at Xbox. "Great games remain at the center of these franchises and at the heart of Xbox. XP will partner with the best creative minds across our studios, along with trusted partners, to build on that foundation and create more ways for people to experience the worlds they love."
A large focus of Microsoft's newest investment will be in cross-media partnerships, looking particularly at film and TV. It seems lots of publishers are eyeing up the film industry, no doubt buoyed by the massive success of titles like the Super Mario Bros. and Super Mario Galaxy movies (which have earned $1.36bn and $1bn, respectively) and Sony's recently released Resident Evil movie (which is tracking at $280m+ at the time of writing). Xbox has had its own notable successes on the big screen, too: last year A Minecraft Movie amassed more than $550m (£415m) in two weeks, immediately setting up a sequel.
Xbox has also experimented with TV in the past, too. Fallout is the highlight for the company at the moment, with Fallout Season 2 boasting 83 million viewers tuning in during its first 13 weeks of release. Less successful was Paramount's divisive Halo TV show, which was cancelled after two seasons. A question that springs to my mind when reading this is: where will we go next? There are plenty of Xbox franchises that'd make for good TV; Perfect Dark, Fable, and maybe even a Forza story in the style of Sony's peculiar Gran Turismo show would work. I know the initial run at a Halo TV show was a bit of a flop, but I'd love to see a limited series on the Fall of Reach. It'd make some fine prestige television. We know there's a Gears of War film and a Sea of Thieves film in production, too.
Elsewhere, there's Xbox Places. This is the arm of the company that'll oversee the Minecraft theme parks that are opening in the US and UK that so far represent over £85m of investment from Mojang and Xbox. They're expected to open 'between 2026 and 2027'. Will we hear about more real-life locations that'll fall under the 'Places' banner? It remains to be seen.
All these initiatives will no doubt require staffing, which is such to be a sore subject for any of the staff that have been impacted by wide-ranging cuts at Microsoft and Xbox over the past few years. Given the contraction of its game studios and software business, is Xbox trying to recoup costs by pursuing other avenues for growth? It certainly seems like it.

It looks like the GTA 6 leaker, 'CyberLeek' is back - and this time the infamous leaker has posted a 25-minute video of footage from Rockstar's upcoming game that even features nude scenes, including a fully naked Jason, and a topless Lucia. Eurogamer has seen the video, and it appears to be legitimate - and, as is now traditional, has 'CyberLeek's' emblem overlaid on top of the footage.
Note: obviously, there are some mild spoilers pertaining to what you might do in GTA 6 below.
Most of the new video takes place around the Thrillbilly Mud Club, and follows the protagonist duo as they prepare for a dirt-biking event - buying new clothes and participating in the off-road driving tournament. Jason wanders around a garage and chooses which bike he'd like to rent to take part in the festivities.
Then, for over 10 minutes of the footage, Jason is completely naked. 'CyberLeek' shares footage of the character riding around on a dirtbike fully nude, with his penis out and seemingly reacting realistically to the world with its own dedicated physics. It's worth noting at this point that whoever is playing the game seems to have access to a dev menu - they spawn in a tank out of thin air - so it's possible that nudity in this way is not available in-game, and has rather been allowed in this dev version of the game. My instinct is that you will be able to be nude in-game, though; it's rated 18+ and it's a Grand Theft Auto game, the series has previous, and a ratings board has confirmed there'll be 'full on sex scenes'.
Towards the end of the footage, we see Lucia in a thong and topless, preparing for a base dive (it looks like the same one that was initially shown in the Netflix reveal) - albeit this time it's night time, and she is mostly naked.
'CyberLeek' went to ground for a while following the Netflix reveal, with today's post taking many by surprise. Will we see more from the leaker in the coming days? It's anybody's guess at this point.

item.description:
How do you revive a series like Hellraiser? When your source material spans four decades and multiple mediums, all with wildly differing tones (and fans), what stays, what goes? Where would you even begin? It's a question developer Saber Interactive seems to struggle with throughout Hellraiser: Revival and the result is a messy, uneven, but earnest, and often fascinating sort of tribute that, boldly, goes back to the start.
Clive Barker's 1986 novella The Hellbound Heart, the genesis of the Hellraiser series, is a queer horror classic; a story of obsession and addiction, loosely inspired by the gay BDSM scene. Later Hellraiser movies would see the series devolve into silliness, iconic villain Pinhead (played by Doug Bradley, who briefly returns here) becoming a quipping counterpart to the Freddies and Chuckies of the time. But Saber seems to have more literary ambitions, drawing heavily on Barker's original themes for its tale of two lovers and their encounter with the Cenonbites; extradimensional beings from a realm where agony and ecstasy are interwined.
It's a story that starts with sweaty softcore sex and soon descends into flesh-ripping violence, setting protagonist Aiden against a quasi-religious, extreme BDSM cult as he desperately attempts to rescue his girlfriend Sunny back from Hell. Unfortunately, their relationship is so immediately toxic, it's hard to get emotionally invested in this critical narrative throughline.
Tonally, Hellraiser is a strange game. Instead of artfully orchestrated scares, Revival's horrors rely on a grim procession of fused and rended flesh, as relentless as it is effectively offputting. But the ceaseless bodily destruction sits awkwardly alongside villains so deliriously flamboyant, they'd be twiddling their moustaches if it weren't for their masks. And attempts at eroticism and sensuality quickly short circuit amid the dildo-strewn nightclub neon, where extras spit out porn-calibre line readings of flat innuendo. Narratively, it's also a bit of a mess; too obvious and too incoherent by turns, clumsily walking through a minefield of complex ideas - most obviously, the intersection of sex and violence - with all the subtly and nuance of a double-A FPS with an interactive paddle spanking scene. But to its credit, it just about manages to avoid feeling exploitative, and there is, I think, an earnestness to Revival that carries it through.
This is the work of a studio, you sense, with a genuine love of the source material - and a desire to do it justice too. And that manifests in a game willing to take some unexpectedly big swings. They don't always work, but at least it's interesting. Take combat, for instance. Revival is, foundationally at least, a fairly bog standard FPS, and it's not long before an early dalliance with perfunctory stealth makes way for more confrontational action. You start with a pistol and, slowly, your arsenal swells to include a shotgun, a revolver, an SMG, and more; an enigmatic old woman intermittently setting up stall to sell you new toys and upgrades (it's not the only time Revival feels like it's channeling Resident Evil 4). Eventually, you're mowing down the Unworthy armed with laser-sight pointers and incendiary shells, which should be the absolute antithesis of horror, but Saber just about makes it work.
For starters, Aiden moves with a satisfying sense of physicality. He wobbles when he runs, sidesteps with weighty momentum, and, when the melee weapons come out, he bludgeons and slices with sickeningly tangible abandon. And while Revival is undoubtedly action-heavy, Saber still finds tension in withholding. Weapons break, ammo is short, and even the most basic enemies take a good few hits to bring down. Throw in armoured foes which need to be stripped first - either with a swing of something heavy or a particularly aggressive blast - and every combat encounter feels like it's perpetually teetering on the brink of disaster. But Revival strikes a good balance between stressful and unduly punishing.
And while I don't love the modern day proliferation of crafting systems, the focus on furious scavenging here feels additive. It heightens the sense of last-gasp desperation as you pocket anything and everything, in the hope you've got enough to eke out a couple more health packs or bullets when things go wrong. Your limited inventory space, meanwhile, forces some tough choices as you frantically shuffle, stash, or abandon items, optimistically Tetrising together the most effective arsenal from the scraps at your disposal.
Later, Hellraiser's iconic puzzle box - here, the Genesis Configuration - essentially becomes a gravity gun, so you can fling sawblades, spikes, even fireballs, shredding through multiple bodies as one. And if you're short on the Suffering needed to power it, near-dead enemies wobble on their last legs so you can gruesomely syphon it out of them. Combat's pilfered parts might feel Resident Evil by way of Half-Life and Doom, but at its best, Hellraiser finds an enjoyably ad hoc rhythm of its own - creating showdowns of pure frantic panic as you scramble to juggle weapons that seem to empty their ammo in seconds, as you furiously scan your surroundings for something pointy to use as a projectile, and delve into your inventory, desperately jettisoning stuff to make space for whatever feels most pressing right now.
The trouble is Revival spends a lot of time failing to make the most of its tools. Particularly in the first half of the game, progress feels like a linear sequence of encounters that are over before they've even begun, so quick to wrap up there's no space to settle into anything like a rewarding combat rhythm. (Conversely, bosses tend to drag on a touch too long.) And it tends to make for a lot of uninspiring busywork in a game that's already erratically paced, often adopting the relaxed meandering of a walking sim. And while I get what Saber is going for with its inventory system, constantly having to pause a big fight to manually switch weapons in and out of the limited equip-slots feels like a faff too far, and kills momentum.
What saves it though are the set-pieces: cabin in the woods ambushes where you're suddenly expected to furiously board up the windows while the Unworthy pour in; locked-room face-offs against grasping horrors that can melt into the floor while you've barely space to turn, and swerves into smoky hide-and-seek creeping. There's rarely a big encounter that doesn't throw in a new twist, and it lends Revival an infectious unpredictability that permeates everything.
Few of Hellraiser: Survival's ideas are original, admittedly (it even nicks Skyrim's lockpick mini-game), but it's hard to be bored in a game that pingpongs so incessantly. And just when its real-world action feels like it's starting to sag, proceedings are usually buoyed by Aiden's extra-dimensional jaunts into the Labyrinth, where the Cenobites and their demonic deity Leviathan reside. Revival is a good-looking game, but it's here - in Hellraiser's Escher-esque, non-Euclidean nightmare of endless, impossibly configured stone - that Saber's artistry really shines.
I am, I'll admit, a sucker for video games that delight in impossible spaces, so there's definitely some bias here. But the Labyrinth's confounding abstractions are a real high point; trading uneven combat for a shift into puzzles, platforming, and pursuit.
It's rarely complicated stuff: you'll dodge vicious blades and sneak around violently whirring traps; you'll stealth to avoid the watchful eye of Leviathan, or use your Genesis Configuration to shift monolithic blocks and create new paths. But when the blocks you're shifting are vast spirals of grinding stone, or staircases that seem to unfold on themselves, spinning around as gravity shifts on its axis, sending the world into a disorientating vortex of movement and sound, it massively elevates the whole thing. Likewise, there are a handful of arresting PT-inspired sequences, where memories melt into unreality under the Leviathan's gaze, and even some genuinely effective chase sequences as you flee from a relentless Chatterer - the Labyrinth endlessly reconfiguring itself around you in real-time. These are perhaps the standout moments; melding spectacle and tension without descending into frustration.
Hellraiser: Revival is not, I don't think, a great game. It's too messy and inconsistent to earn that accolade. And there are times - particularly in its uneven opening half - when I wouldn't even say it's a good game. Tonally and narratively, it's all over the place, stumbling where nuance is required and struggling to create a strong emotional throughline. It borrows so much for its gameplay grab-bag that it often struggles to find its own identity whenever the Cenobites and the Labyrinth are off-screen. Its action sometimes sags too. But slowly, it begins to find a more confident rhythm. Its combat and encounters grow more engaging, making the most of its tools. And as the line between the Labyrinth and the real-world blurs, the erratic tone settles and the best bits of both halves start to merge. Hellraiser: Revival might be scrappy and inconsistent, but it's entertaining, and even when it's not, it's at least fascinating. Which probably also describes the series as a whole. A bit of pleasure, a bit of pain - how apt!
A copy of Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival was provided for this review by Saber Interactive.

item.title: World of Warcraft: Forever's developers have announced drastic visual changes to the game's new Skyborne race following passionate community feedback. These include new in-game models that better represent the game's early MMO aesthetic, much to the community's delight. Read more
item.description:
World of Warcraft: Forever's developers have announced drastic visual changes to the game's new Skyborne race following passionate community feedback. These include new in-game models that better represent the game's early MMO aesthetic, much to the community's delight.
The World of Warcraft community first caught wind of these changes during a recent episode of the official World of Warcraft: Forever podcast, in which senior game designer Josh "Aggrend" Greenfield acknowledged impassioned feedback of the Skyborne humanoid and druid character models. While he didn't have anything to announce then, he said the team "hoped to have something more substantive to say pretty soon". And "pretty soon" now seems to have arrived.
The blog post detailing these changes, published on the World of Warcraft website, starts by establishing the team's aim to "uphold the original WoW era aesthetic" while offering more choice in how they experience Azeroth. It then admits that some of the team's ideas around the visual fidelity of certain new additions missed the mark: specifically the Skyborne models. The blog notes: "The Skyborne are from an exotic environment, and their Druid forms reflect that, but we don't want that to be dissonant with the visual language of other creatures in the world."
Both versions of the Skyborne elves in World of Warcraft: Forever will be altered to better align with the rest of the game. The blog shows side-by-side comparison before-and-after images, which highlight the models' softness being removed, colour saturation lowered, and more detailed fur textures added.
Perhaps what's more exciting, especially to World of Warcraft: Forever players who value retro visuals, is word of planned changes to the standard definition models. The blog agrees with feedback that the standard definition Skyborne models could feel "jarring" next to the game's legacy races, and confirms that new standard definition models are in the works, with a planned release in early 2027. For now, an image of work-in-progress characters was included. Look at those sharp angles! You could cut an apple on those.
Shimmying over to the popular World of Warcraft Reddit, and the mood is similarly joyful. Notably, many players are expressing their appreciation at the WoW Forever team's eagerness to respond to community feedback so quickly and openly. One popular thread is titled: "Ignore the toxic positivity. Disregard the brigaders. Keep giving feedback. Keep being vocal. Forever team is GOATed and they're listening." The thread highlights not only these changes, but also the recent decision by Blizzard to lower the rarity of dungeon loot so quest rewards aren't devalued, and the decision to change the races' headshots in the character creator from Modern WoW's headshots to those found in Classic WoW.
"The fact that they tweaked these rather minor things and even changed the icons is honestly in my eyes monumental," wrote user Ubberman. "Who are these people? That is an exceedingly high response rate and for rather minor things that only add to the feel. If they keep this up for even a year, WoW Forever will genuinely be the best World of Warcraft version to date. Genuinely."
World of Warcraft: Forever may still only be in beta, but it's already proving mighty popular. The server cap had to be increased due to player demand, and early critique of this introductory version of the upcoming MMO - including ours - is largely positive. WoW Forever launches in full on 4th November.

item.title: Google and Unity yesterday announced new generative-AI game-making platforms designed to make and shape games by inputting text prompts. Google's product is called Playground and is available for testing now, if you live in the US, and Unity's product is Unity Spark and is "coming soon". Read more
item.description:
Google and Unity yesterday announced new generative-AI game-making platforms designed to make and shape games by inputting text prompts. Google's product is called Playground and is available for testing now, if you live in the US, and Unity's product is Unity Spark and is "coming soon".
Their side-by-side announcements are more than coincidence. Google Playground will work with and integrate Unity Spark when "creators" want to "expand their concepts" with "robust, professional-level mechanics, high-fidelity 3D capabilities", Google's Playground blog post said.
Given that, there's a sort of two-tiered approach going on here. Google Playground is the entry level platform, a much more - excuse me while I throw-up on myself - 'vibe-coded' idea origination tool. It's the sort of thing you plug a load of words into the text box, presumably while marvelling at your own creativity and taking lifestyle selfies on a beach somewhere, while Google Playground builds a fairly simple game. Then, when you're happy with it, and AI-prompting a post on LinkedIn about your career change, you can share the game with other Playground users.
Said Google: "Games are one of the most creative forms of expression, and the gaming community keeps growing. But game creation has historically been limited to a select group of people who have technical experience and knowledge of complex game engines. Today, we're introducing Playground, an experimental gaming platform that lets you create, play, and share custom games. Playground lowers the barriers to creation, so bringing game ideas to life can now be as easy as describing it through a few prompts — no coding experience required."
Unity Spark, on the other hand, is a more complicated affair. There are text prompts but they work more as shortcuts or helpers within Unity's more traditional game engine package, so it's not just a 'whack a load of text in, sit back, and create' kind of affair. Indeed, in an interview with Gamefile, Unity boss Matt Bromberg underlined this point, stating that Spark was not about "one-shotting" game development.
"I'm not denigrating folks who are interested in one-shotting things," Bromberg said. "I think there's a level of excitement and enthusiasm about what the technology can do. And maybe that's just a way of people celebrating it." But, he said: "Unity Spark is not going to be for everyone. There are many people who don't have the patience and ambition to make something real.
"Asking the AI to reproduce a game that has already been made does not make you [Hideo] Kojima. It doesn't make you a famous game developer any more than typing the first paragraph of War and Peace into your word processor makes you Tolstoy."
One of the major features of Unity Spark is the ability to co-create games with other people in real-time, and a Unity Spark video showed this in action, with a pair of people - Mari and Theo - making their dream game, Space Corridor. It's a pretty rubbish sci-fi shooter, albeit one that's made quickly, and we see obvious complexity in the engine while it's being made.
Gamefile saw Unity Spark demonstrated live, and apparently it pulled assets from Unity's Store for use. Where Google Playground pulls art and assets from, we don't know - Google didn't say. Gamefile also quizzed Bromberg about the carbon footprint of Spark, which presumably requires a lot of power to build games. Could there be an estimated carbon footprint cost next to requests? "We hadn't considered that," Bromberg replied. "That's something worth considering."
Unity isn't the first game engine to heavily incorporate generative-AI, though. Epic Games revealed a big gen-AI push this summer for its ubiquitous game engine Unreal, incorporating large language model support into its current generation of Unreal, and targeting foundational integration of LLMs for Unreal Engine 6. Even Capcom is evolving its in-house RE Engine "for the AI generation", to incorporate help with coding, QA testing, and more.

item.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an absolute delight to play, and for fans of the Burnout games, it can feel like coming home. That's hardly surprising given that Fuse Games, the creators of Galactic Racer, contains an awful lot of DNA from Burnout's old home at Criterion. Read more
item.description:
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an absolute delight to play, and for fans of the Burnout games, it can feel like coming home. That's hardly surprising given that Fuse Games, the creators of Galactic Racer, contains an awful lot of DNA from Burnout's old home at Criterion.
But what does it mean for a game to feel like Burnout? And how do you make a game that channels the junky, battered-tech side of Star Wars? I spoke to some of the people behind Galactic Racer to find out.
So here's a quick chat with Matt Webster, the CEO of Fuse Games, along with Kieran Crimmins, the creative director at Fuse, and Craig Derrick, executive producer at Lucasfilm Games. It touches on everything from "game feel" and emotion to board game prototypes and Richard Donner's Superman.
I had a moment when I started my first game, and I set off, and I waited until I would normally press boost in Burnout, and then I pressed the boost button from Burnout, and it did exactly what I thought it was going to do if I had been playing Burnout. I think a lot of people know your lineage from Criterion. They will be thinking along the same lines as I was, and I wondered how you feel about people having that experience: the rediscovery of the Burnout boost.
I think that what you're describing is not just the boost mechanic: press a button and go faster. It's everything that happens when you depress that button. We reduce it down into: button goes down, speed goes up. But there is clearly more going on there. But yeah, the game feel part is extraordinarily important. It's a throughline throughout the entire experience. Because if you can suspend your disbelief on a primary sensory level, then we can immerse you so much more powerfully in everything else that's going on as well.
Does this search for game feel help to dictate the way you approach Star Wars? This is the Star Wars of brilliant but sometimes decrepit technology that can go really fast but can also break at the worst moment.
Matt Webster: That's not us. That's this wonderful galaxy that we get to play in. It's all there for us to lean into. The game is a combination of our love of racing and our love of Star Wars. We come at it as fans, and we see those details too, and it's just that we have the wonderful privilege to be able to put some of them into action. The tactile nature: bashing something to get it to work. I always call that "touch sensitive", right? That leads to flicking levers and doing button combinations at race start. That's never getting old. That's the thing that connects you into the tactility of the galaxy.
When I look at Burnout, there's a grippiness to that game. In Paradise, you feel like your wheels are almost traveling in grooves in the road. So when you approach a game where you don't have wheels, how do you get a sense of connection to the road?
Matt Webster: What you're just describing again is an attention to game feel that I think we have a very particular point of view on. It just so happened in something like Burnout, for us at least, the best way around a corner in a car is sideways with all four wheels straight. But that's actually quite difficult to do. To deconstruct the intention there: the average driver doesn't think they're an average driver, right? We all think that we're incredible. And that's the fantasy we're trying to do here. The starting fantasy is to be an incredible racing pilot.
And actually it's pretty liberating to be decoupled from tyres on tarmac. We can do different things, exciting things. We can amplify the vertical. We can amplify the angles. But it's all built on some pretty significant foundations. Which are: if you could invent a levitating jet engine on Earth, it would behave in this way because we built a simulation to deliver it. And the reason you do that is because we've all got an innate understanding of the physical world around us. There is a physical simulation going on there. And it's inspired by everything that we've seen about Star Wars, from the podracers to the land speeders to the speeder bikes to every vehicle that we've seen there.
When you pay so much attention to game feel and you control the experience in that way to give players a very specific sensation, what's it like to then add Roguelite features and give players control over what they build? Does that feel like giving away control or does it feel like something else?
Matt Webster: Fundamentally we define the container. And because those rulesets and those systems are cared for and crafted and balanced. We want to push the genre forward. I [often] talk about [how] arcade is not the absence of depth. It's your route into it. And then we reveal that depth in accessible and approachable ways for you to go and play.
Kieran Crimmins: And the things you're [building your vehicle with], we would call our player story generator. The point of creating all these physical toys, which is essentially what they are from a fundamental level, is so that you can play with them like you would play with your toys. That means stacking them on top of each other, creating something that you wouldn't expect. But then it reacts in a way that feels physical and real and expected, but it's also yours. What we try to do is create moments of emotion for players. I mean, game design, on this fundamental level, is systems that create emotions, right? So we target emotions from Star Wars. We target emotions from racing. We target emotions from the story, and then we turn them into play. We turn them into interactive experiences. So we don't need to curate everything that happens along a timeline because we give you a set of toys that are the experiences that create that racing thrill.
Is it hard to put all those pieces together? The vehicle parts and upgrades?
Kieran Crimmins: We like many things. We have loads of ideas, and we have references and emotions that we're trying to get to. But you can't know if you've got game feel. You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system. So we just try and get into [the] prototype [stage], get it into our players' hands. See if they're feeling those emotions. So rather than worry about whether it's the right set of things, we worry about getting it as a play experience as quickly as possible and seeing if it feels right. And that's how we ended up with those things [we have to play with in the game]. They were actually part of the original board game for the early prototype.
I've got to stop you. Tell me about the board game prototype.
Matt Webster: It's a prototyping story. What's the fastest way we can get ideas down and then talk about them. You know, modern engines are so capable that you can do a lot of in software, but there's still something [about that that is] not as fast as getting a written idea down. From a board game perspective, you sort of decouple yourself from a particular prototype and you're talking about moment–to–moment.
Kieran Crimmins: There's a prototyping tool for every kind of system that you want to prototype, and the one that you pick should be the one that gets you there the quickest, and gets you to validate the emotion the quickest. So when it came to upgrades and meta progression, I can do a board game in a day. I mean, I say "board game". A lot of it is Post–its and a scribble and some dice. But we're trying to validate those feelings as quickly as possible. So you just pick the best tool for the moment.
I'm struck by how much you talk about emotions in your game design process.
Craig Derrick: Emotions are the new verbs, you know. Kieran, you're going to nail this, but I'm just going to say, when we're talking about the experience of play and the agency that you want to feel through those moment–to–moment experiences, how can you not describe it as an emotional state?
Kieran Crimmins: I think you're absolutely right. I think it's fair to say, what's the point in all this if you're not feeling something? Yeah. Like whether that's games, walking through the park, whatever it is, that is the ultimate goal: to create some strong emotions, and that be some sort of reflection of your thing of playing. It's always been at the heart of everything we do everywhere I've worked where we make games.
Matt Webster: Maybe as an industry we don't talk about it enough, but when we talk about games, we're actually talking about how it made us feel. So it is always is all about emotion, whether it's the sensory feel or the or the emotional feel or the what's motivating me. I tell this story a lot. One of the original superhero movies was the original Superman, directed by Richard Donner. I remember watching the DVD extras, and he was sat in front of his production desk talking about the movie, and behind him was this massive word, and it said 'Verisimilitude." I had to look it up. It was graffitied on the wall behind him.
And essentially, it means the truth of the thing, or the truth of the heart. It stuck with me a lot, right? Because what he said was, "If you don't believe a man can fly, it doesn't matter what else we do. If, fundamentally, you don't believe a man can fly, nothing's going to work."
So if you don't believe that you are in the Star Wars galaxy, that you are piloting this land speeder around at 600 kilometers an hour. If you don't believe that, then it doesn't matter what story we're doing, the awesome stuff that we're doing in the paddock, and this sports story that we're telling. If you don't believe that at the heart, then we can't do all the other stuff. And that brings us back to that starting point of why that sort of stuff is really important, on that very base, foundational level.

item.title: Last year, we learned that Xbox cancelled a reboot of Perfect Dark. The game, in development at The Initiative, was cancelled as part of 2025's wave of wide-ranging cuts at Microsoft and Xbox. In 2026, of course, things have only gotten worse for the company. Read more
item.description:
Last year, we learned that Xbox cancelled a reboot of Perfect Dark. The game, in development at The Initiative, was cancelled as part of 2025's wave of wide-ranging cuts at Microsoft and Xbox. In 2026, of course, things have only gotten worse for the company.
Over the past 24 hours, leaked gameplay footage of the Perfect Dark reboot has surfaced online, giving us a glimpse at what could have been. The gameplay, first unearthed by MP1ST, shows off a few of the different weapons protagonist Joanna Dark would have been able to use, as well as a few different environments she'd have been sneaking and fighting her way through. MP1ST claims the footage it uncovered - which has since spread around various social media accounts - comes from a VFX artist that "has previous experience working on various gaming franchises". The authenticity of the footage is hard to ascertain but it certainly looks the part.
The Perfect Dark footage includes the bare-bones layouts of some level environments, a little gunplay testing (this looks to be particularly early), a couple of abilities, and even a few pieces of destructible fruit. Delicious.
LEAKED | Perfect Dark — 2 mins of GameplayPerfect Dark is a cancelled first-person shooter game that was under development by The Initiative and Crystal Dynamics pic.twitter.com/w5adSFPFem
The reboot of Rare's Perfect Dark series was first announced back in December 2020, and was in development at new Xbox Game Studios developer The Initiative. The game became infamous for its slow and seemingly difficult development, with Tomb Raider developer Crystal Dynamics at one point recruited to help with it. In May 2024, reports suggested "little meaningful progress" had been made since the game's unveiling and that the reboot was in "a very rough state".
We got our first trailer for the Perfect Dark game just after that report, however, which seemed to reignite belief in the project. Alas, one year later, reports of its demise began to circulate. The game would have reportedly taken on an episodic structure, and after its cancellation, there was a suggestion that Take-Two might have snapped up the rights to the game, but this apparently fell through.

item.title: The Coalition, the Microsoft-owned studio behind Gears of War: E-Day, Gears 4 and Gears 5 has mostly survived the wide-ranging cuts and layoffs initiated by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma in her attempt to bring the gaming division back to profitability. Read more
item.description:
The Coalition, the Microsoft-owned studio behind Gears of War: E-Day, Gears 4 and Gears 5 has mostly survived the wide-ranging cuts and layoffs initiated by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma in her attempt to bring the gaming division back to profitability.
But as Eurogamer reported, now that Gears of War: E-Day has shipped, many within The Coalition fear they're going to be laid off shortly afterwards, potentially missing out on bonuses.
Now, in an interview with the BBC, studio head Mike Crump was asked about the report and whether cuts are planned for the Canadian studio. Crump didn't offer specifics about the future of the studio, however.
"What I say to myself, what I say to the team, is we just we need to focus on the things that we can control," said Crump. "For us that's about shipping a great game that people are going to love and I feel like, as a team, we've done that."
E-Day has been fairly well-received by critics and embraced by players, boasting the series' best numbers on Steam. In the Eurogamer E-Day campaign review, Dom Peppiatt said the game proves there's still life left in the aging franchise.
But the big question is whether that is going to be enough to keep The Coalition safe and convince Xbox to invest in a future project. E-Day is an Xbox console exclusive - a decision reportedly hastily made just before the game's big summer reveal - which limits its audience and sales potential.
"Gears has been an exclusive franchise to Xbox for 20 years now. It's sort of entwined deeply with the brand," said Crump.
Asked how the studio measures success, the studio head said that while numbers are important, there's more that gets taken into account. Said Crump, "We measure things like, are we showcasing the platform? Are we pushing the hardware to its limits? Are we showcasing what the Xbox is capable of?
"Our goal basically is to be the best-looking game on the Xbox and really show the industry what's possible with our hardware."
After shipping Gears 5 in 2019, it took The Coalition seven years to develop and release Gears of War: E-Day. To that end, the studio boss believes E-Day makes for a "great foundation" for future sequels, and promises the next game "will not take nearly as long" to develop. The Coalition has not announced any future projects.

item.title: Star Wars: Zero Company maker Bit Reactor is bringing back developers who were furloughed ahead of launch. Read more
item.description:
Star Wars: Zero Company maker Bit Reactor is bringing back developers who were furloughed ahead of launch.
"This week, we started the process of returning more of our team back to work at Bit Reactor, an important step forward in our continued support for Zero Company," studio CEO Greg Foertsch said in an online statement from today. "Having to ask team members to step away after we navigated unexpected business developments outside of our control and so close to launch was an incredibly difficult decision, but one that was necessary to help us eventually bring as many people back as possible.
"This team means a tremendous amount to me, and I am incredibly proud of what we have accomplished together," Foertsch continued. "Thank you to our fans for the incredible response to the game and for supporting us along this journey. We look forward to sharing more updates regarding Bit Reactor and Zero Company soon."
Weeks before the acclaimed tactics game came out, the studio reportedly furloughed around 80% of its workforce, which means "most" staff were sent on a leave of absence without pay or benefits. Bit Reactor seemingly ran out of cash to pay its workers, following a legal battle between co-founders Alison Kelly and Foertsch, who has sole ownership of the company.
Bit Reactor doesn't specify how many of its developers have returned to work, though Game File recently reported that more than half of the studio's overall headcount is back on payroll, citing a source familiar with the situation. A fair number of workers are still left in limbo, then.
Star Wars: Zero Company was a big hit right out of the gate, quickly selling over 1m copies and winning over fans by transporting XCOMs best bits to a galaxy far, far away. Here's hoping the rest of the team can come back soon.

item.title: Sony reportedly wants to revive a selection of its long-dormant PlayStation classics with the help of smaller third-party developers, and a new Ape Escape game is apparently up first. Read more
item.description:
Sony reportedly wants to revive a selection of its long-dormant PlayStation classics with the help of smaller third-party developers, and a new Ape Escape game is apparently up first.
The tidbit comes courtesy of The Jeff Gerstmann podcast, where Gerstmann said that a new Ape Escape was on the way from Evening Star, the independent team who made the fan-favorite Sonic Mania before forming their own studio and releasing the surprisingly delightful Penny's Big Breakaway. VGC corroborated the podcast's claims, as well.
"I don't think this game is close to being out or anything like that, but I guess it's been almost a year since we started talking about Ape Escape," Gerstmann said. "Who is making it? That's a good question. My understanding is that it’s an external studio. You know, because people were immediately like, 'Oh, Team Asobi (Astro Bot) is making it.' My understanding is that an external team has been working on that… Evening Star. I heard that they were working on it."
VGC also reported that PlayStation isn't stopping with Ape Escape, either - the console maker is apparently keen to work with other outside developers on some of its legacy IP. It's the same blueprint Sony used for 2025's Everybody's Golf: Hot Shots, which was handled by Bandai Namco.
Ape Escape was a beloved series of 3D platformers during PS1 and PS2 generations, and had players running around levels and catching chaos-causing apes with special gadgets. The last mainline game in the series was 2005's Ape Escape 3, though a lovely playable tribute was also included in Astro Bot.
Speaking of, Astro Bot was a good reminder of just how many classic games PlayStation is sitting on, so there's certainly a lot to choose from. There's already been rumours of a new Killzone game from People Can Fly (Outriders, Gears of War: Judgement), for one. Which comebacks would you like to see? I'm keeping my fingers crossed for Sly Cooper.

item.title: Microsoft has revealed the first batch of games coming to Xbox Game Pass this month, though subscribers only have a week left to try the award-winning Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 before it waves goodbye. Read more
item.description:
October's undisputed headliner is one of last year's hottest games, EA's Battlefield 6. The large-scale shooter broke series records when it dropped, selling over 7m copies in three days and instantly topping Steam's best-seller charts. Post-launch updates and a surprisingly-involved Top Gun collab have kept the game chugging into this year too, despite layoffs at Battlefield Studios back in March.
The other highlights include seven all-new games launching into Game Pass straight away. Time-loop metroidvania Echo Weaver, road trip adventure game Forever Ago, co-op survive-em-up Deep Dish Dungeon, first-person soulslike Valor Mortis, cute photography romp Bluey's Happy Snaps, co-op roguelike Chained Beast, and city-builder (on the back of a space whale) Beyond These Stars slot into the service on the same day as their full launches.
But Game Pass giveth and Game Pass taketh away. This month's group of leavers include the widely-acclaimed and hugely-celebrated RPG, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, which debuted on Game Pass early last year. Some personal favorites, like Donut County and Pacific Drive, aren't sticking around either.
For more, check out our full guide to Xbox Game Pass and see every game in the service.
I have one eyebrow tentatively raised for Deep Dish Dungeon's moody, old-school world, if I can fend off the hordes in Gears of War: E-Day for long enough, that is - are you guys interested in any of the newcomers?

item.title: State of Decay studio Undead Labs has spoken out after rebuying its independence and leaving Xbox last month, revealing it has "got to make some changes" to State of Decay 3 because of layoffs it suffered as a result. Read more
item.description:
State of Decay studio Undead Labs has spoken out after rebuying its independence and leaving Xbox last month, revealing it has "got to make some changes" to State of Decay 3 because of layoffs it suffered as a result.
Studio boss Phillip Holt said this during a wide-ranging conversation with The Game Business, in which he detailed the studio's shifting priorities now it has no "boss" to respond to other than its audience, and while explaining why the co-op zombie survival game seems to have been in development for ages.
"We're pretty close to finishing this game," Holt said. "And there's a lot in it. I think folks that saw us at Gamescom can attest to that. I think our alpha players can attest to that. And obviously, with a significant number of people leaving the company, we've got to make some changes. But I don't think we're dramatically addressing scope in that way."
State of Decay 3 currently has a vague release date of "2027", announced this summer, which allows Undead Labs some scheduling wiggle-room. But the game was originally revealed all the way back in 2020, before slipping out of view for a long time, leading people to wonder about what was going on.
"I don't think it's taken that long, actually," Holt remarked, when speaking about the game's long development. "If you measure it from when State of Decay 2 shipped, yeah, we're approaching eight years. If you measure it from our first trailer with the infamous zombie deer, that's also a long time. I got myself in a little bit of trouble by saying we didn't really have a team working on the game at that point, which wasn't entirely true, we had a very small team. We've had a small team on the game since maybe 2020. But development didn't really pick up until 2022 or 2023."
But why did Undead Labs announce the third State of Decay game so early? The answer is eerily prophetic, and it's to do with the spending spree Microsoft was on when it acquired Undead Labs in 2018 - the same spending spree that saw it acquire Ninja Theory, Compulsion Games, and Playground Games (two of which are also no longer a part of Xbox). Holt wanted to announce State of Decay 3 before Undead Labs was "swallowed up or divested" by the rest of a much bigger gaming division, he said.
"I didn't think Microsoft was done being acquisitive," Holt explained, "and I didn't think they'd continue buying small developers - I assumed they'd start buying big things. I was a little worried about getting swallowed up or divested before we had a chance to present to the world what we were working on. So, it was a bit of a marker on the table. I was saying, 'State of Decay 3, we're announcing it, the audience knows it's in development, and here's a trailer to demonstrate our vision.'"
Undead Labs was eventually earmarked for divestiture this summer when Xbox announced its major restructuring. At the time, Undead Labs was said to have "entered terms to join new ownership", but that new-ownership deal - as in the case of Ninja Theory - never actually materialised. "We had a lot of interest," Holt assured The Game Business, but when he heard other studios were doing management buyouts, he submitted one for Undead Labs, "and Microsoft thought that would be a good idea".
Holt wouldn't say how many people were laid off as a result of the studio downsizing to operate independently, "because these are our friends and colleagues and it was a total heartbreak to have to part ways". "I would hate to reduce the impact to those individuals to a number or statistic," he said. But he insisted the studio had "everything we need to ship State of Decay 3", and that its mission was now even clearer.
"Inside of a larger company, you serve multiple objectives and you have directives that you need to achieve," Holt said. "Now it's just: make the best possible game. Of course, inside Xbox, that was also the primary objective. But it's just a cleaner, clearer line of sight to the audience. I don't have a boss. The success or failure of the company is down to whether we create something an audience will support.”
State of Decay 3 will still launch on Game Pass on day one, and Holt praised Xbox's subscription service as being partly responsible for the series' ongoing success, which has apparently seen it reach 25 million players over its lifetime. "I don't know that we'd be in the place we are today if not for the Game Pass audience," he acknowledged. "Even today, we have several thousand people coming through the door every day."

item.title: Call of Duty recently kicked off a week of Modern Warfare 4 DMZ news, which brought us a first look at the "action extraction" mode and some insight into developer Infinity Ward's guiding philosophy. Read more
item.description:
Call of Duty recently kicked off a week of Modern Warfare 4 DMZ news, which brought us a first look at the "action extraction" mode and some insight into developer Infinity Ward's guiding philosophy.
Although more reveals are promised, what's been confirmed so far left one of the biggest questions hanging over DMZ unanswered. Namely, whether the mode is going to offer a PvE-only playlist for those not keen on fighting other players. Dedicated PvE is something that inevitably gets brought up with every new extraction shooter, as we've recently seen with Arc Raiders, Bungie's Marathon, and Escape from Tarkov before that. So, does Modern Warfare 4's DMZ have anything to offer PvE players? Infinity Ward hasn't said, but players picked up on some clues seen in recent trailers.
This all started with episode seven of From the Ward, a behind-the-scenes feature that takes us inside the studio. The focus of that episode was entirely on DMZ and it naturally showed a lot of gameplay. At minute 7:34 into the video, we see the deployment screen with four options. Three of the four are discussed, and have on-screen descriptions - except for Single Squad Mission, which suspiciously has neither.
For players eager to get any confirmation of a PvE-only mode, it was a welcome surprise. The name implies the lobby is limited to a single squad, meaning it's a game players can only join through an invite.
Players took to Reddit and X to ask if the name actually implies what they thought it does, with some tagging the official Call of Duty account directly. While many agree with the basic definition, others believe it's referring to something else.
"Could be a solely PvE mode for DMZ. Would be great if true as I'd rather not have to spend however long getting decent gear just to get wiped by a super," one Reddit user wrote.
Other players, however, think it has to do with DMZ's Lieutenant Hunts, a high-risk encounter type. Defeated Lieutenants drop their Dog Tag, and the player has to extract safely with it for the hunt to count. The counter theory, then, is that Single Squad means only one tag will drop, meaning only a single squad (or player) can extract with it. This is admittedly a weaker explanation, but in the absence of an official description, players are left to come up with their own.
Disrupting that state of affairs was another official trailer, released just one day later. The DMZ Dynamic Ops trailer spotlights one of the four options we referred to earlier. However, when the trailer shows the deployment screen, Single Squad is suspiciously absent.
So what does this mean? It's likely the trailers show different builds of Modern Warfare 4. It's not hard to believe an older build of the game having Single Squad, before it was either removed or pushed back to a post-launch season.
It's also possible Single Squad is an option only available to new players to help with onboarding. The player in the From the Ward video is level 5, compared to level 28 in the most recent trailer. It's not uncommon for multiplayer games to offer low-stress modes to ease newcomers into the experience - rival shooter Battlefield 6 has done it, and many battle royale games, such as Fortnite, limit new players to bot-only matches in their first few levels.
All of that speculation and discourse has once again highlighted the need for a PvE mode. In recent weeks, Infinity Ward did what many thought was unthinkable in adding a silly skin off toggle in Warzone and changing double XP tokens to count down in-match and not in real-time. I could see PvE DMZ being next on that list - even if it's planned for sometime after release.
"Really strange for me why they didn't add PvE from [the] start. Just watch [Escape from] Tarkov with both modes, everybody looks happy with that," wrote another.
DMZ is part of Modern Warfare 4, and is available at its launch on 23rd October for PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2.
